Rudd has been in several comedies written, directed or produced by Judd Apatow, considered one of the leaders of the "bromance" trend with his softer, more openly emotional male characters. Segel has also been in Apatow projects -- including last year's "Forgetting Sarah Marshall" -- and he stars in the TV series "How I Met Your Mother," which finds plenty of humor in male bonding. Segel observes that what helps the films work is the discomfort of two men trying to talk about their emotions while hoping to maintain a dispassionate, hard-edged, prototypically manly façade. And he knows he's good at bringing out that discomfort in his co-stars. "Judd Apatow told me that my special skill was that I am able to maintain my likability while getting incredibly close to the creepy line, and that's what I should try to cultivate," he said. "That's what he does," Rudd noted. "He just holds [the moment] a little too long." "It's the fraction of a second too long that makes people uncomfortable," Segel added. "It was a real treat for me, to be honest for a minute, to play this character, because I've played sort of a puppy dog guy in 'Forgetting Sarah Marshall,' and on ['Mother'] I play a husband, you know, a loving husband," he said. "So to get to play a character who is a bit more of a man of mystery was very exciting for me." In real life, claims Segel, he even has a man cave. "It's filled with puppets," he said. "And I keep wondering why I don't have a girlfriend. I'm like, 'hey, this is my house; come check it out. This is where I keep my 40 puppets.' ... I think that I have a reputation for being weird because of that." But he quickly turns serious and maintains that "I Love You, Man" does have a message to go along with its comedy. "I think we both had something to learn from each other," he said. "Paul's character had to learn that it's all right to take a little distance from your significant other and have some dude friends and someone to vent to about things you can't necessarily talk about with your girl." "Sometimes buddies hold a mirror up to the way you behave in ways that relationships with the opposite sex don't," Rudd said. "Yeah, and my character had to learn that maybe it's time to grow up a little bit," Segel added. So, this "bromance" thing, allowing a few feelings to show. Perhaps it's not so bad after all? Rudd says that the idea has its upside, despite its name. And he's glad it's been successful. "That's us in a nutshell, not macho, not tough," he said. "I think that we've all been kind of drawn to real stories, you know, characters that hopefully people can relate to and what's funny about just certain insecurites and just certain things in life. "They could easily be dramatic," he pointed out. "Just less fart jokes."

NEW YORK (CNN) — They’ve been called “bromances”: buddy films and television shows—such as the movies *Pineapple Express* and *The 40-Year-Old Virgin*—that center on nonsexual but deeply felt friendships between two or more men.

Jason Segel and Paul Rudd star in *I Love You, Man*, which opens Friday. The forthcoming film appears to fit the bill. In it, Rudd plays a man who needs a best man for his wedding but has never made any male friends. Enter Segel as Sydney Fife, whom Rudd’s character, Peter Klaven, pursues on several “man-dates” that ultimately threaten his relationship with his fiancée, played by Rashida Jones.

But don’t call the film a “bromance” in front of Rudd and Segel.

“We hate that word,” Segel told CNN.

“It was not part of the lexicon while we were filming,” Rudd added.

Still, both actors have ample experience in the, shall we say, guy-pal genre. Rudd has appeared in several comedies written, directed, or produced by Judd Apatow, who is widely regarded as one of the leading figures of the “bromance” trend, known for portraying softer, more openly emotional male characters.

Segel has also worked on Apatow projects—including last year’s *Forgetting Sarah Marshall*—and stars in the television series *How I Met Your Mother*, which finds plenty of humor in male bonding.

Segel observes that part of what makes these films effective is the discomfort that arises when two men try to discuss their emotions while still attempting to maintain a dispassionate, hard-edged, conventionally masculine façade. And he knows he has a talent for drawing out that discomfort in his co-stars.

“Judd Apatow told me that my special skill was that I am able to maintain my likability while getting incredibly close to the creepy line, and that’s what I should try to cultivate,” he said.

“That’s what he does,” Rudd noted. “He just holds [the moment] a little too long.”

“It’s the fraction of a second too long that makes people uncomfortable,” Segel added.

In *I Love You, Man*, Segel’s character is rougher and looser than his characters in *Forgetting Sarah Marshall* and *How I Met Your Mother*. He welcomed the change.

“It was a real treat for me, to be honest for a minute, to play this character, because I’ve played sort of a puppy dog guy in *Forgetting Sarah Marshall*, and on [*Mother*] I play a husband, you know, a loving husband,” he said. “So to get to play a character who is a bit more of a man of mystery was very exciting for me.”

In real life, Segel claims, he even has a man cave.

“It’s filled with puppets,” he said. “And I keep wondering why I don’t have a girlfriend. I’m like, ‘Hey, this is my house; come check it out. This is where I keep my 40 puppets.’ ... I think that I have a reputation for being weird because of that.”

But he quickly turns serious, maintaining that *I Love You, Man* does have a message to accompany its comedy.

“I think we both had something to learn from each other,” he said. “Paul’s character had to learn that it’s all right to take a little distance from your significant other and have some dude friends and someone to vent to about things you can’t necessarily talk about with your girl.”

“Sometimes buddies hold a mirror up to the way you behave in ways that relationships with the opposite sex don’t,” Rudd said.

“Yeah, and my character had to learn that maybe it’s time to grow up a little bit,” Segel added.

So, this “bromance” thing—allowing a few feelings to show—perhaps it is not so bad after all?

Rudd says the idea has its upside, despite the name. And he is glad it has been successful.

“That’s us in a nutshell: not macho, not tough,” he said. “I think that we’ve all been kind of drawn to real stories, you know, characters that hopefully people can relate to, and what’s funny about just certain insecurities and just certain things in life.

“They could easily be dramatic,” he pointed out. “Just less fart jokes.”

NEW YORK (CNN) — The term “bromance” has often been used to describe movies and television shows centered on close, non-sexual friendships among men — projects such as “Pineapple Express” and “The 40-Year-Old Virgin.”

The upcoming film “I Love You, Man,” opening Friday and starring Paul Rudd and Jason Segel, seems to fall into that category. In the movie, Rudd plays Peter Klaven, a groom-to-be who realizes he has no male friends and therefore no one to serve as his best man. That changes when he meets Sydney Fife, played by Segel. Peter begins going on a series of “man-dates” with Sydney, but the new friendship starts to create problems in his relationship with his fiancée, played by Rashida Jones.

Just don’t use the word “bromance” around Rudd and Segel.

“We hate that word,” Segel told CNN.

Rudd added that the term “was not part of the lexicon while we were filming.”

Even so, both actors are well acquainted with comedies about male friendship. Rudd has appeared in several films written, produced or directed by Judd Apatow, who is widely seen as a major figure in the “bromance” wave because of his gentler, more emotionally open male characters. Segel has also worked on Apatow productions, including last year’s “Forgetting Sarah Marshall,” and he stars on the sitcom “How I Met Your Mother,” a show that often finds comedy in the bonds between men.

According to Segel, much of the humor in these stories comes from watching men struggle to discuss their feelings while trying to preserve a detached, tough, traditionally masculine image. He also recognizes that he has a talent for making that awkwardness stand out in scenes with other actors.

“Judd Apatow told me that my special skill was that I am able to maintain my likability while getting incredibly close to the creepy line, and that's what I should try to cultivate,” Segel said.

“That’s what he does,” Rudd said. “He just holds [the moment] a little too long.”

“It’s the fraction of a second too long that makes people uncomfortable,” Segel said.

In “I Love You, Man,” Segel’s Sydney is more rugged and freewheeling than the characters he played in “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “How I Met Your Mother.” Segel said he was happy to take on that kind of role.

“It was a real treat for me, to be honest for a minute, to play this character, because I’ve played sort of a puppy dog guy in ‘Forgetting Sarah Marshall,’ and on [‘Mother’] I play a husband, you know, a loving husband,” he said. “So to get to play a character who is a bit more of a man of mystery was very exciting for me.”

Segel also joked that, in real life, he has his own man cave.

“It’s filled with puppets,” he said. “And I keep wondering why I don’t have a girlfriend. I’m like, ‘hey, this is my house; come check it out. This is where I keep my 40 puppets.’ ... I think that I have a reputation for being weird because of that.”

Still, Segel said the movie is not only about jokes; he believes it carries a message as well.

“I think we both had something to learn from each other,” he said. “Paul’s character had to learn that it’s all right to take a little distance from your significant other and have some dude friends and someone to vent to about things you can’t necessarily talk about with your girl.”

Rudd agreed that friendships can reveal things romantic relationships may not.

“Sometimes buddies hold a mirror up to the way you behave in ways that relationships with the opposite sex don’t,” he said.

“Yeah, and my character had to learn that maybe it’s time to grow up a little bit,” Segel added.

So maybe this whole “bromance” idea — men letting a few emotions show — is not such a terrible thing after all. Rudd said that, despite disliking the label, the concept has value, and he is pleased audiences have responded to it.

“That’s us in a nutshell, not macho, not tough,” he said. “I think that we’ve all been kind of drawn to real stories, you know, characters that hopefully people can relate to and what’s funny about just certain insecurites and just certain things in life.

“They could easily be dramatic,” he added. “Just less fart jokes.”

**Paul Rudd and Jason Segel helped define the “bromance.” They’re still proud of what it said about male friendship**

Nearly 15 years after *I Love You, Man* turned “slappin’ da bass” into a comedy catchphrase, Paul Rudd and Jason Segel’s 2009 buddy comedy remains one of the clearest examples of a very specific movie era: the rise of the “bromance.”

The film, directed by John Hamburg, starred Rudd as Peter Klaven, an affable real estate agent who realizes he has no close male friends as his wedding approaches. Segel played Sydney Fife, the freewheeling, Rush-loving bachelor who becomes Peter’s unexpected best friend. What could have been a simple odd-couple comedy became something a little more lasting: a mainstream movie about how awkward, meaningful and emotionally vulnerable male friendship can be.

At the time, the word “bromance” was everywhere — shorthand for a close, affectionate, non-romantic relationship between men. *I Love You, Man* didn’t invent the term, but it helped cement it in pop culture.

The movie arrived during a run of comedies associated with Judd Apatow and his collaborators that often put male friendship, insecurity and arrested development at the center of the story. Films like *The 40-Year-Old Virgin*, *Knocked Up*, *Superbad*, *Forgetting Sarah Marshall* and *Pineapple Express* mixed raunchy humor with a surprising amount of sincerity. Rudd and Segel were key figures in that comedy ecosystem, appearing in or alongside many of those projects.

What set *I Love You, Man* apart was that its central relationship wasn’t a romance, a workplace rivalry or a family bond. It was simply about one grown man trying to learn how to make a friend.

Rudd’s character is almost painfully polite, emotionally contained and eager to do the “right” thing. Segel’s Sydney is impulsive and confident, but not portrayed as a cartoonish party animal so much as someone who gives Peter permission to loosen up. Their friendship is funny because it is socially clumsy — full of misread signals, overenthusiastic nicknames and uncomfortable attempts at masculine cool — but it is also gentle.

That gentleness has helped the movie age well. Beneath the jokes about man-dates and awkward phone calls is a question that still feels relevant: Why is it so hard for some men to say they need each other?

In many Apatow-adjacent comedies of the 2000s, men bonded through video games, weed, fantasy sports, sex jokes or pop-culture obsessions. But the best of those films also suggested that beneath the immaturity was a longing for connection. The humor often came from characters who didn’t have the vocabulary for emotional honesty but were trying, in their own clumsy way, to get there.

*I Love You, Man* pushed that idea to the foreground. Peter isn’t trying to win a woman — he already has a loving fiancée, played by Rashida Jones. He’s trying to build an identity outside of romance and work. The film treats that need as legitimate, not pathetic.

Rudd and Segel’s chemistry made the premise work. Rudd’s comic strength has long been his ability to play embarrassment without cruelty; he lets audiences laugh at Peter while still rooting for him. Segel, meanwhile, brings warmth to a character who could have easily been written as just a chaotic man-child. Together, they make Sydney and Peter’s friendship feel odd, fast-moving and oddly believable.

The word “bromance” itself has always carried a slightly comic charge, as if male affection needs a wink or a qualifier to be acceptable. But the emotional core of *I Love You, Man* is more straightforward: friendship can be intimate without being romantic, and men benefit from having people in their lives with whom they can be unguarded.

That idea has only become more openly discussed in recent years, amid broader conversations about loneliness, mental health and the ways men are socialized to hide vulnerability. What seemed in 2009 like a clever comedy hook now reads as part of a larger cultural conversation.

The film’s ending — Peter and Sydney reunited at the wedding, their friendship fully acknowledged in front of everyone — plays like a romantic-comedy finale, only for a platonic relationship. That was the joke, but also the point. The movie gave a male friendship the emotional weight typically reserved for a love story.

And in doing so, Rudd and Segel helped make a case that still resonates: saying “I love you, man” might sound funny, but it doesn’t have to be a punchline.

LOS ANGELES — Paul Rudd and Jason Segel are happy to talk about friendship, awkward first impressions and the strange rituals men invent to avoid saying how they feel.

They are less enthusiastic about one particular word.

“I don’t know,” Rudd says with a laugh when asked about “bromance,” the increasingly popular label for close male friendships in movies and television. “It always sounds like it’s winking too hard. Like it’s embarrassed by what it’s describing.”

Segel nods. “Exactly. It makes it feel like there has to be a joke in front of it before two guys can say, ‘Hey, I care about you.’”

Their new comedy, **“I Love You, Man,”** opening this month, is built around that very idea. Rudd plays Peter Klaven, a successful real-estate agent who has just gotten engaged to Zooey, played by Rashida Jones. There’s only one problem: Peter realizes he doesn’t have a close male friend to serve as his best man.

Enter Sydney Fife, played by Segel — a laid-back, blunt, Rush-loving bachelor who seems to have no trouble saying whatever is on his mind. What follows is part buddy comedy, part romantic comedy and part portrait of an adult man trying, with considerable discomfort, to make a new friend.

“It’s funny because dating has rules, or at least people think it does,” Rudd says. “But making friends as an adult can be even weirder. There’s no script. You don’t know if you’re calling too soon. You don’t know if asking someone to hang out sounds desperate.”

Segel says that awkwardness is what drew him to the story.

“There’s something very honest about a guy realizing, ‘I don’t have the people in my life I thought I did,’” he says. “The movie is ridiculous in places, but that feeling is real.”

The film arrives at a time when male friendship has become a reliable engine for Hollywood comedy. From “The 40-Year-Old Virgin” to “Superbad” and Segel’s own “Forgetting Sarah Marshall,” studios have found box-office success in stories about men behaving badly, growing up slowly and occasionally discovering emotional vocabulary along the way.

But Rudd says “I Love You, Man” is less about a trend than about a simple comic premise.

“The central relationship is between two guys, but it’s not a parody of a romantic comedy,” he says. “It borrows some of that structure, sure — the meet-cute, the misunderstandings, the big emotional moment — but it’s really about intimacy in friendship. And how hard that can be when you’re not used to it.”

That may be why both stars resist the shorthand.

“‘Bromance’ makes it sound like the friendship is funny because it resembles romance,” Segel says. “But friendships are their own thing. They can be intense and meaningful and complicated without needing that comparison.”

Rudd adds, “Also, it just sounds like a word someone made up in a marketing meeting.”

In “I Love You, Man,” Peter’s attempts to find a best man lead to a series of disastrous “man-dates,” including uncomfortable dinners, mismatched personalities and the kind of over-sharing that can turn a casual meeting into a social crime scene. Rudd, who has built a career playing likable men under various degrees of panic, says he recognized Peter’s strain immediately.

“He’s not a loser,” Rudd says. “He’s got a job, he’s in love, he’s functioning. He just missed this one part of life. And once he notices it, he can’t stop noticing it.”

Segel’s Sydney, by contrast, seems to have too much ease. He is the sort of guy who can walk into an open house, offer unsolicited life advice and somehow leave with a new friend.

“Sydney is comfortable in his own skin, maybe to a fault,” Segel says. “He doesn’t have Peter’s filter. Part of the comedy is that Peter wants what Sydney has, but Sydney also needs Peter. He’s not just the cool guy who fixes everything.”

The film co-stars Jon Favreau, Jaime Pressly, Andy Samberg and J.K. Simmons, and is directed by John Hamburg, who co-wrote “Meet the Parents” and directed “Along Came Polly.” Like those films, “I Love You, Man” finds comedy in the anxiety of social performance — the terror of saying the wrong thing, or worse, trying so hard to say the right thing that it comes out mangled.

For Rudd and Segel, the movie’s title gets closer to the point than any trendy label.

“That phrase is funny because it’s direct,” Rudd says. “A lot of guys will say anything else first. They’ll make a joke, quote a movie, punch you in the arm. But sometimes the simplest thing is the hardest thing to say.”

Segel smiles. “And if people leave the movie and call their friends, that’s great. Just don’t call it a bromance.”

Rudd laughs. “Yes. Please. We’re begging you.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a celebrity interview story about Jason Segel and Paul Rudd promoting “I Love You, Man,” focusing on their Apatow-related careers, Segel’s “creepy line” humor, his puppet-filled man cave, and the film’s take on guy friendships.
counterfactuals.output:
**Jason Segel and Paul Rudd Find the Funny in Friendship in “I Love You, Man”**

By the time Jason Segel and Paul Rudd sit down to talk about *I Love You, Man*, they seem less like co-stars promoting a studio comedy and more like two guys who wandered into an interview after making each other laugh in the hallway.

Which, in a way, is exactly the point.

Their new film, directed by John Hamburg, is built around a simple but surprisingly underexplored premise: What happens when a perfectly functional adult man realizes he has no close male friends? Rudd plays Peter Klaven, a sweet, successful real estate agent whose engagement exposes a glaring problem — he has no best man. Segel plays Sydney Fife, the free-spirited, Rush-loving, emotionally unfiltered guy who enters Peter’s life and becomes his unlikely candidate for best friend.

It’s a buddy comedy, yes, but with the structure of a romantic comedy: awkward first encounters, nervous phone calls, jealousy, misunderstandings, and one man wondering whether he has come on too strong.

For Rudd and Segel, that emotional awkwardness is where the comedy lives.

“Male friendship can be really strange,” Rudd says. “There are all these things guys don’t say, or don’t know how to say, and somehow that becomes the language of the friendship.”

Segel nods. “There’s a whole courting process,” he says. “You meet a guy and you think, ‘I like this guy. Do I ask him to hang out? Is that weird? Do I wait?’ It’s the same insecurity as dating, except nobody wants to admit that.”

That vulnerability is familiar territory for both actors, whose careers have been shaped in part by the Judd Apatow comedy universe — a loose family of films and television shows that helped redefine mainstream comedy by mixing raunch, sincerity, emotional panic, and improvisational looseness.

Rudd was already a familiar face from *Clueless*, *The 40-Year-Old Virgin*, and *Knocked Up*, where he perfected a comic persona equal parts handsome everyman and quietly unraveling neurotic. Segel, meanwhile, built his reputation through Apatow’s cult series *Freaks and Geeks* and *Undeclared*, later breaking through with *Forgetting Sarah Marshall*, which he also wrote. That film established him as a leading man with a peculiar specialty: making humiliation feel strangely generous.

Segel has an unusual gift for locating what he calls “the creepy line” — that delicate border between endearing and alarming.

“The funniest place to be is right before someone says, ‘Okay, that’s too much,’” Segel says. “If you go way past it, it stops being funny. But if you’re right on that line, where the audience is laughing and also thinking, ‘Should I be worried about this guy?’ — that’s a fun place.”

Sydney Fife, his character in *I Love You, Man*, lives almost entirely on that line. He’s confident but oddly intense, friendly but boundary-free, the kind of man who will invite you into his world with such enthusiasm that you may not realize until later how bizarre that world is.

And then there is the man cave.

Sydney’s home base is a shrine to arrested adolescence and personal freedom: instruments, pop-culture artifacts, and a proudly curated space where adulthood seems to have been negotiated rather than fully accepted. Most memorably, it includes puppets — a detail that feels especially Segel-esque, given the actor’s well-known affection for puppetry and the handmade weirdness it brings to comedy.

Segel lights up when talking about that kind of environment.

“I love when a character’s private space tells you everything,” he says. “Sydney is a guy who has figured out exactly how he wants to live, for better or worse. There’s something really admirable about that, even if it’s also ridiculous.”

Rudd laughs. “Peter walks into that space and it’s like he’s seeing an alternate version of masculinity. He’s so tightly wound, and Sydney is just completely unembarrassed.”

That contrast is the engine of the movie. Peter is polite, controlled, and painfully eager to do friendship correctly. Sydney is instinctive, blunt, and often inappropriate. Together, they create a comic rhythm that depends not on one character being “normal” and the other being “crazy,” but on the idea that both are incomplete in opposite ways.

Rudd’s gift has always been making discomfort look effortless. As Peter, he turns small social failures into full-body events: a botched nickname, a weird goodbye, a voice mail that should have ended 30 seconds earlier. He is playing a man who is good at life on paper but helpless at the casual rituals of male bonding.

“Peter doesn’t know the rules,” Rudd says. “And the joke is that nobody really knows the rules. Some guys are just better at pretending.”

The film’s comedy also comes from treating male intimacy as something both ordinary and absurdly fraught. Peter and Sydney go on “man dates.” They jam to Rush. They share secrets. They fight. They miss each other. The language of romance is applied to friendship, not as parody exactly, but as a way of acknowledging that deep friendships can be just as emotionally significant.

“There’s this idea that guys are supposed to be low-maintenance,” Segel says. “But friendships take maintenance. You have to show up. You have to be honest. You have to risk being embarrassed.”

That idea places *I Love You, Man* squarely within the Apatow-adjacent tradition that helped make both actors stars: comedies about people who are immature not because they don’t care, but because they care and don’t know what to do with it. The jokes may involve bodily functions, awkward oversharing, or Segel pushing a moment into near-creepiness, but underneath is a genuine interest in how adults connect.

Rudd says that sincerity is what keeps the comedy grounded.

“If the friendship doesn’t matter, then the jokes don’t matter,” he says. “You have to believe Peter really needs this person in his life, even if he doesn’t understand why at first.”

Segel agrees. “The best comedy, for me, comes from someone wanting something badly. Peter wants a friend. Sydney wants connection too, even if he acts like he doesn’t need anything. That’s funny because it’s human.”

Their own rapport makes the film’s central relationship easy to buy. In conversation, Rudd is dry and quick, often tossing off a joke under his breath; Segel is open, expansive, and slightly mischievous, the kind of comic presence who seems delighted when a thought gets weird. Together, they have the relaxed timing of performers who trust each other enough to let scenes breathe.

That ease was essential for a movie built around the awkwardness of trying to become close.

“You can’t fake liking someone,” Rudd says. “Well, you can, technically. It’s called acting. But comedy is easier when there’s real affection there.”

Segel grins. “That’s the nicest thing you’ve ever said to me.”

“Don’t make it creepy,” Rudd replies.

Segel pauses just long enough.

“Too late.”

It is a small exchange, but it captures why *I Love You, Man* works: the joke is not simply that men are bad at expressing affection. It is that affection is risky, funny, necessary, and occasionally very weird. The movie gives male friendship the full romantic-comedy treatment — the nerves, the thrill, the heartbreak, the reunion — and finds something both silly and sincere in the process.

For Segel and Rudd, that combination is the sweet spot.

“Guys need friends,” Segel says. “They need people who know them and call them on their stuff and also want to sit around and listen to music or do something dumb. That’s not a small thing.”

Rudd nods. “Sometimes the dumb thing is the important thing.”

In *I Love You, Man*, the dumb thing might involve awkward slang, a jam session, an overdesigned man cave, or a moment that hovers right on Segel’s beloved creepy line. But beneath it all is a surprisingly tender argument: finding a best friend as an adult can be just as confusing, exposing, and life-changing as falling in love.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a full-length entertainment news article beginning “NEW YORK (CNN) --” about bromance movies like “Pineapple Express” and “The 40-Year-Old Virgin,” then segue into Paul Rudd and Jason Segel’s new comedy “I Love You, Man.”
counterfactuals.output:
NEW YORK (CNN) -- In the modern romantic comedy, the path to happily ever after has usually been paved with meet-cutes, misunderstandings and last-minute dashes to the airport. But in recent years, Hollywood has found another kind of love story hiding in plain sight: the bromance.

From the hazy, high-stakes friendship of “Pineapple Express” to the emotionally stunted but oddly tender ensemble of “The 40-Year-Old Virgin,” comedies about male friendship have become one of the most reliable subgenres in mainstream film. They trade candlelit dinners for video games, action-movie marathons and awkward confessions between men who may be more comfortable making jokes than admitting they need one another.

The appeal is not difficult to understand. Bromance movies let audiences laugh at male insecurity while also acknowledging it. Their heroes are often grown men who can hold jobs, maintain apartments and sometimes even fall in love — but who struggle mightily with intimacy, vulnerability and basic emotional vocabulary when it comes to friendship.

In “Pineapple Express,” Seth Rogen and James Franco turned a dealer-customer relationship into a chaotic buddy odyssey. The film wrapped its friendship story in explosions, marijuana smoke and action-comedy parody, but beneath the mayhem was a familiar emotional arc: two guys realizing they genuinely care about each other, even if they can only express it while running from danger.

“The 40-Year-Old Virgin,” directed by Judd Apatow, helped set the template for the current wave. Steve Carell’s Andy was the romantic center of the film, but the movie’s comic engine came from his circle of male co-workers, played by Rogen, Paul Rudd and Romany Malco. Their advice was frequently terrible, their conversations were wildly inappropriate, and yet their loyalty gave the movie its warmth.

Those films, along with “Superbad,” “Wedding Crashers” and other male-bonding comedies, helped shift the language of studio comedy. Male friendship was no longer just a side plot on the way to the altar. It became the main event.

Now Paul Rudd and Jason Segel are taking that idea to its logical conclusion with “I Love You, Man,” a comedy built around a man searching not for a bride, but for a best man.

Rudd stars as Peter Klaven, a successful real estate agent who has just become engaged to Zooey, played by Rashida Jones. Peter seems to have his life in order, but there is one glaring problem: He has no close male friends. When wedding planning forces him to confront the empty space where his groomsmen should be, Peter begins a series of increasingly uncomfortable “man dates” in search of a best friend.

Enter Segel’s Sydney Fife, a relaxed, outspoken investor with a love of Rush, open houses and blunt personal advice. Sydney is everything Peter is not: unfiltered, socially fearless and unconcerned with appearing polished. Their friendship quickly becomes the central relationship of the film, complicating Peter’s engagement in ways that echo the beats of a traditional romantic comedy.

That is part of the joke — and part of the point. “I Love You, Man” borrows the structure of a romance and applies it to male friendship. There is the first meeting, the spark of connection, the honeymoon phase, the conflict and, inevitably, the grand gesture. The title itself plays like a punch line because it says directly what many of these characters spend entire movies trying not to say.

Rudd, long a scene-stealer in comedies such as “Anchorman,” “Knocked Up” and “The 40-Year-Old Virgin,” brings his familiar mix of charm and discomfort to Peter. He is at his funniest when trapped inside his own politeness, smiling through social panic and inventing slang that collapses the moment it leaves his mouth.

Segel, known for “How I Met Your Mother” and “Forgetting Sarah Marshall,” plays Sydney with a looser energy. He is not simply the wild friend who teaches the uptight hero to loosen up; he is also a man with his own loneliness and eccentric code. The comedy comes from the mismatch between Peter’s neediness and Sydney’s confidence, but the friendship works because both characters are looking for connection.

The film arrives at a moment when Hollywood comedies have become increasingly comfortable poking fun at masculinity without entirely mocking it. The men in these movies are often ridiculous, but their feelings are treated as real. They may communicate through nicknames, insults, sports references or classic-rock fandom, yet the emotional stakes are sincere.

That balance has been crucial to the success of the bromance. Too much irony, and the friendship feels hollow. Too much sentiment, and the comedy loses its edge. The best entries in the genre understand that affection between men can be funny precisely because it is often expressed indirectly.

“I Love You, Man” also benefits from placing a woman at the center who is not merely an obstacle. Jones’ Zooey is not threatened by Peter having friends; she is concerned because he does not. That twist helps separate the movie from comedies in which male bonding is framed as an escape from adult relationships. Here, friendship is part of growing up.

The supporting cast adds to the film’s comic texture, with appearances from actors including Jon Favreau and Jaime Pressly as a married couple whose bluntness offers a more abrasive version of intimacy. But the movie ultimately belongs to Rudd and Segel, whose chemistry gives the story its easy rhythm.

Like many bromance comedies, “I Love You, Man” finds humor in embarrassment: bad dates, misread signals, forced bonding and the strange etiquette of adult friendship. Making friends after a certain age can feel uncomfortably similar to dating, and the movie mines that idea for both laughs and recognition.

That may be why the bromance has endured beyond a passing trend. Beneath the raunchy jokes and absurd situations is a surprisingly relatable anxiety. How do adults make close friends? How do men say they care about each other without feeling exposed? And why is it sometimes easier to propose marriage than to ask another guy to hang out?

For years, romantic comedies have insisted that finding “the one” is the ultimate happy ending. Movies like “Pineapple Express” and “The 40-Year-Old Virgin” suggested there might be another kind of relationship worth celebrating, one built on loyalty, shared jokes and the occasional terrible decision.

With “I Love You, Man,” that idea moves fully into the spotlight. It is a comedy about marriage, but its central courtship is between two men trying to figure out whether they can be best friends. In the world of the bromance, that question is every bit as dramatic — and just as funny — as love at first sight.
